tEn: Snap CEO Evan Spiegel on AR Glasses, AI Anxiety and the Future of Social Media
tZh: Snap CEO 埃文·斯皮格尔谈 AR 眼镜、AI 焦虑与社交媒体未来
sEn: Snap co-founder and CEO Evan Spiegel discusses the new Specs AR glasses, the smartphone's future, AI fears and whether social media faces a tobacco-style reckoning.
sZh: Snap 联合创始人兼 CEO 埃文·斯皮格尔畅谈新一代 Specs AR 眼镜、智能手机的未来、AI 焦虑，以及社交媒体是否会迎来类似烟草诉讼的清算。

consensus.en: Computing should move into the 3D world, be shared, and hands-free, making it more human.
consensus.zh: 计算应融入三维世界、可共享且解放双手，从而更人性化。

consensus.en: AI will make software businesses vulnerable, but network effects and differentiated services provide resilience.
consensus.zh: AI将使软件企业变得脆弱，但网络效应和差异化服务提供韧性。

consensus.en: AI-driven productivity gains are real: code changes doubled while engineering team shrank 30%.
consensus.zh: AI驱动的生产力提升是真实的：代码变更翻倍，而工程团队缩减30%。

consensus.en: Investing in understanding user behavior and intervening before harm is the future of safety.
consensus.zh: 投资于理解用户行为并在伤害发生前干预是安全的未来。

consensus.en: Collaboration among platforms, including signal sharing, is essential for teen safety.
consensus.zh: 平台间合作，包括信号共享，对青少年安全至关重要。

consensus.en: AI is unlikely to kill us all; the anxiety is amplified by prominent leaders' warnings.
consensus.zh: AI不太可能杀死我们所有人；焦虑被知名领袖的警告放大了。

contrarian.en: Smart glasses should be unmistakable, not disguised as normal glasses, to build trust.
contrarian.zh: 智能眼镜应显而易见，而非伪装成普通眼镜，以建立信任。

contrarian.en: Snapchat has a measured positive impact on well-being, unlike other social media services.
contrarian.zh: 与其他社交媒体服务不同，Snapchat对福祉有可测量的积极影响。

contrarian.en: AI is very likely to be better at controlling computers than humans, changing form factors.
contrarian.zh: AI很可能比人类更擅长控制计算机，从而改变设备形态。

contrarian.en: The backlash against AI is not new; Snap removed AI-generated content early due to user negativity.
contrarian.zh: 对AI的反弹并不新鲜；由于用户负面情绪，Snap很早就移除了AI生成内容。

contrarian.en: Billionaire taxes like Prop 40 reduce tax revenues over time, burdening average taxpayers.
contrarian.zh: 像Prop 40这样的亿万富翁税长期会减少税收，加重普通纳税人负担。

contrarian.en: Advertisers will continue to value platforms that demonstrate conversions, regardless of agent traffic.
contrarian.zh: 无论智能体流量如何，广告商将继续看重能证明转化率的平台。

turns.en: Hello and welcome to the interview from Times Tech. I'm Katie Prescott.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎收听 Times Tech 的访谈。我是 Katie Prescott。

turns.en: And I'm Danny Fortson here in London and this week we've been talking to Evan Spiegel, the co-founder and chief exec of Snap at the Times Tech Summit. Evan co-founded the messaging app Snapchat, as it was known then, in 2011. And today it has nearly 500 million daily users and made him one of the world's youngest billionaires at the age of just 24.
turns.zh: 我是 Danny Fortson，在伦敦为您报道。本周我们在 Times Tech 峰会上采访了 Snap 的联合创始人兼首席执行官 Evan Spiegel。Evan 于 2011 年联合创立了当时名为 Snapchat 的通讯应用。如今它拥有近 5 亿日活用户，这也让他在年仅 24 岁时成为世界上最年轻的亿万富翁之一。

turns.en: So people know Snap for the app and Snapchat as you just referenced, but they're launching their new iteration of their venture Specs, which is a pair of AR glasses. And we all got a chance to try them at this year's Times Tech Summit. So it was quite funny cuz there were lots of people in the audience
turns.zh: 大家都知道 Snap 是因为它的应用和 Snapchat，但正如你刚才提到的，他们正在推出其新迭代产品 Specs，这是一副 AR 眼镜。我们在今年的 Times Tech 峰会上都有机会试戴。挺有趣的，因为观众席上有很多人

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: walking around with these junior bosses with these glasses sort of stabbing at virtual buttons in the air.
turns.zh: 戴着这些眼镜走来走去，像小老板一样在空中戳虚拟按钮。

turns.en: Did you try them?
turns.zh: 你试过了吗？

turns.en: I did actually. I tried them before the summit. I went along to a hotel in Mayfair to try them on. And there was this enormous window looking out over Piccadilly with a whole bunch of construction workers in the building on the other side. So God knows what they thought we were up to, wandering around this room sort of pinching and poking at the air. I did all sorts of things with them. I played a game of dominoes
turns.zh: 我确实试了。我在峰会前试的。我去梅菲尔的一家酒店试戴。那里有一扇巨大的窗户俯瞰皮卡迪利大街，对面建筑里有一群建筑工人。天知道他们以为我们在干什么，在房间里走来走去，对着空气捏捏戳戳。我用它们做了各种各样的事情。我玩了一局多米诺骨牌

turns.en: Oh.
turns.zh: 哦。

turns.en: with one of the engineers. So you know, you're both wearing glasses and you can see the dominoes between you. I used it with Google Docs, so it sort of projects a screen in front of you and you can sit with a keyboard, the idea being like in a cab or on a train or whatever and type away. It's hard to imagine you walking around with them in your day-to-day life. They are heavy.
turns.zh: 和一位工程师一起。所以你知道，你们都戴着眼镜，可以看到彼此之间的多米诺骨牌。我还用它配合 Google Docs，它会在你面前投射一个屏幕，你可以坐着用键盘，想法是在出租车或火车上之类的地方打字。很难想象你在日常生活中戴着它们走来走去。它们很重。

turns.en: getting bullied.
turns.zh: 被欺负。

turns.en: Oh, that wasn't my worry but yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，那不是我的担忧，但是的。

turns.en: I guess my point is they're not like oh, those are smart glasses? Like they're very clearly I mean the way he talked about it which you'll soon hear is like it's effectively they've miniaturized the computer and put it on your face.
turns.zh: 我想说的是，它们不像那种“哦，那是智能眼镜吗？”它们非常明显，我是说，他谈到的方式你很快就会听到，就像是他们有效地将电脑小型化并戴在你脸上。

turns.en: It is extraordinary actually when you think about the amount of technology that is packed into these very small frames. This is not a VR headset by any stretch of the imagination, but they do still feel too large I would say to just be wearing all the time. Too heavy. Yeah. But absolutely extraordinary technology, some of which is developed here in the UK.
turns.zh: 实际上，当你想到这些非常小的框架中 packed 了多少技术，真是非凡。这绝不是 VR 头显，但我会说它们仍然感觉太大，不能一直戴着。太重了。是的。但绝对是非凡的技术，其中一些是在英国这里开发的。

turns.en: yeah, and I think they're he's been at it for a long time like a decade.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为他们已经做了很长时间，大概十年了。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, he was first to this in this sort of social media space way before Meta.
turns.zh: 是的。是的，他在社交媒体领域早在 Meta 之前就率先涉足这个。

turns.en: yeah, and I tried the Apple Vision Pro. I don't know if you tried that.
turns.zh: 是的，我试过 Apple Vision Pro。我不知道你有没有试过。

turns.en: No, I haven't.
turns.zh: 不，我没有。

turns.en: those they're 3,500 goggles
turns.zh: 那些是 3500 美元的护目镜

turns.en: Mm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: with the big headband and it goes over the top of your head as well because it's so heavy and it has a battery pack you have to wear on your waist. And the resolution and what it like the experience is really technologically impressive, but you're kind of like this is way too much money. It's way too heavy. It's just not going to be a thing, right? Whereas Specs are still two grand.
turns.zh: 有大头带，它还越过你的头顶，因为它太重了，而且有一个电池组你必须戴在腰上。分辨率和体验在技术上令人印象深刻，但你会觉得这太贵了。太重了。这不会成为现实，对吧？而 Specs 仍然要两千美元。

turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯哼。

turns.en: They're not cheap obviously. Um, but they're not like basically you know wearing a helmet.
turns.zh: 它们显然不便宜。嗯，但它们不像基本上你知道戴着头盔。

turns.en: quite quite.
turns.zh: 相当相当。

turns.en: but I feels like my sense is that there's still some years to go, right? Before this becomes because then you have the meta ones which we talk about um which are designed by Ray-Ban but are much more kind of paired back
turns.zh: 但我觉得我的感觉是还有几年时间，对吧？在这成为现实之前，因为然后你有 Meta 的那些，我们谈论过，嗯，由 Ray-Ban 设计，但更加精简

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: than what he's trying to do.
turns.zh: 比他试图做的。

turns.en: So we spoke about specs, we spoke about social media and lawsuits um and whether social media is heading for a bit of a reckoning similar to the big tobacco settlements of the 1990s.
turns.zh: 所以我们谈到了 Specs，谈到了社交媒体和诉讼，嗯，以及社交媒体是否正走向类似 1990 年代大型烟草和解的清算。

turns.en: Yes and so here is our wide-ranging and very fun interesting conversation with Evan Spiegel from Snap.
turns.zh: 是的，所以这是我们与 Snap 的 Evan Spiegel 进行的广泛、非常有趣且有趣的对话。

turns.en: Evan I thought we'd start by just going back to the beginning when you started Snap and I know when we were researching this interview we couldn't believe that it was 15 years ago in 2011 I think when you were 21. Just tell us a little bit about the story of the company and how it's changed over the last 15 years.
turns.zh: Evan，我想我们从头开始，回顾你创立 Snap 的时候。我知道我们在研究这次采访时，简直不敢相信那是 15 年前的 2011 年，我想你当时 21 岁。请告诉我们一些关于公司的故事以及过去 15 年它如何变化。

turns.en: If I go back to when we started Snapchat I'd grown up with social media so Facebook was very popular Myspace a lot of us were used to the popularity contest that was social media and it wasn't feeling particularly fun and it also really limited expression because people only posted their most important moments you know the 1 percent of their life that they really felt like sharing with the whole world and it wasn't just Facebook you know X or Instagram all these services came along that were really oriented around public sharing and Bobby and I ended up along with a friend of mine named Reggie having an idea for something really different and it started with disappearing photos but after presenting that to my class they all laughed at me and said that was a terrible idea and you could just take a screenshot anyways. So we pivoted we renamed the service Snapchat we focused on adding creative tools like drawing and captions and what we saw was using it with our friends and my younger sisters and some of their friends that it was a totally new way to communicate that was visual and ever since then, we've just continued to innovate. We can talk about some of the other things we've built. And now we reach 977 million people around the world, including 23 million people here in the UK.
turns.zh: 如果回到我们创立 Snapchat 的时候，我是在社交媒体中长大的，所以 Facebook 非常流行，Myspace，我们很多人都习惯了社交媒体那种人气竞赛，感觉并不特别有趣，而且它也真的限制了表达，因为人们只发布他们最重要的时刻，你知道，他们生活中那 1% 他们真正觉得想与全世界分享的时刻。不仅仅是 Facebook，你知道 X 或 Instagram，所有这些服务都出现了，它们真正围绕公共分享。Bobby 和我，还有我的一位朋友 Reggie，最终有了一个真正不同的想法，它始于消失的照片，但在向我的班级展示后，他们都嘲笑我说那是个糟糕的主意，你反正可以截图。所以我们转型了，我们将服务更名为 Snapchat，我们专注于添加创意工具，比如绘画和字幕，我们看到的是与朋友以及我的妹妹们和她们的一些朋友一起使用它，这是一种全新的视觉交流方式，从那时起，我们就一直在创新。我们可以谈谈我们构建的其他一些东西。现在我们覆盖全球 9.77 亿人，包括英国这里的 2300 万人。

turns.en: Wow, so nearly a billion people. That's quite extraordinary. So specs. For those who haven't tried, what are they and what is the vision for what you're doing with specs?
turns.zh: 哇，所以近 10 亿人。这相当非凡。那么 Specs。对于那些没有尝试过的人，它们是什么，你们对 Specs 的愿景是什么？

turns.en: Yes, you're probably wondering why a photo sharing app would invest for 10 years in a totally new type of computer built into a pair of glasses. And that is because we are obsessed with trying to make computing feel more human. It's one of the things we've done with Snapchat, including with things like Stories, where we put storytelling in chronological order. We had them disappear after 24 hours so people felt like they could change and grow over time.
turns.zh: 是的，你可能想知道为什么一个照片分享应用会投资 10 年在一副眼镜中构建一种全新类型的电脑。那是因为我们痴迷于让计算感觉更人性化。这是我们在 Snapchat 上做的事情之一，包括像 Stories 这样的东西，我们将故事按时间顺序排列。我们让它们在 24 小时后消失，这样人们觉得他们可以随着时间改变和成长。

turns.en: We got rid of the public likes and comments because we thought that inhibited self-expression. And so when we looked at the future of computing and the way that computers are going to change, there were a couple of things that were immediately obvious to us. The first was that it was going to be really important that computing actually lived in the world with you. So computers for the last 20 or 30 years have been just various sized rectangles that are 2D that don't at all reflect the amazing 3D complexity of the world around us. And moreover, force us to look down, I think now for 7 or 8 hours a day on average at these very small flat screens. And so we really wanted to bring computing into the world so that you could look up, you could share that computing experience with see-through lenses with your friends so that they can see what you see. And another huge benefit is that you're hands-free. And that's really important because that means you can work on solving a problem with your hands while you use your computer instead of the model we have today where maybe you're trying to assemble some IKEA furniture and you have to look away at a video on your phone and then go back to building the furniture. And so I think as we look at the way that computing is going to help people solve problems in the future, it's incredibly important that it's overlaid on the world around you, that it's something you can share together with your friends, and it's something you can use hands-free.
turns.zh: 我们取消了公开点赞和评论，因为我们认为那会抑制自我表达。所以当我们展望计算的未来以及计算机将如何改变时，有几件事对我们来说显而易见。第一，计算真正融入你所在的世界将非常重要。过去二三十年，计算机只是各种尺寸的二维矩形，完全不能反映周围世界惊人的三维复杂性。而且，它们迫使我们低头，现在平均每天有七八个小时盯着这些非常小的平面屏幕。所以我们真的很想将计算带入世界，让你可以抬头，可以通过透明镜片与朋友分享计算体验，让他们看到你所看到的。另一个巨大好处是解放双手。这非常重要，因为这意味着你可以一边用手解决问题，一边使用计算机，而不是像今天这样，比如你试图组装宜家家具，却得移开视线看手机上的视频，然后再回去组装家具。所以我认为，当我们展望计算如何帮助人们解决问题时，它叠加在你周围的世界之上、可以与朋友分享、并且可以解放双手，这一点至关重要。

turns.en: And we should say a lot of the technology is developed here in the UK. I think you bought a business in Abingdon, didn't you, to help you sort of build the screen that you see when you put the glasses on.
turns.zh: 我们应该说，很多技术是在英国这里开发的。我想你收购了阿宾登的一家企业，对吧，来帮助你构建戴上眼镜时看到的屏幕。

turns.en: Yeah, don't tell anyone, but the UK has some of the best optical engineers in the whole world. So we're very invested here in the UK and we actually fabricate some of the core components including that glass lens right here in the UK.
turns.zh: 是的，别告诉任何人，但英国拥有全世界最优秀的光学工程师。所以我们在英国投入很大，实际上我们在英国这里制造一些核心组件，包括那个玻璃镜片。

turns.en: But there's still a challenge, isn't there? Because you're basically balancing, as you described it, putting a computer on your face, the battery power you need for that, all of the technology. When do you think it'll get to a stage where they do feel light and you can seamlessly wear them as part of your everyday life in a very comfortable fashion?
turns.zh: 但仍然存在挑战，不是吗？因为你基本上在平衡，如你所说，把电脑戴在脸上，所需的电池电量，所有技术。你认为什么时候会达到这样一个阶段：它们感觉轻盈，你可以非常舒适地无缝佩戴它们作为日常生活的一部分？

turns.en: We've sort of thought 2030 would be the decade that the specs would become capable enough and cheap enough. They're still $2,200 so that's a pretty steep price point and wearable enough. Today there are about 130 g to put that in perspective, Vision Pro is like 2 lb I think all in. So to have this sort of Vision Pro level of capability in a see-through pair of glasses that weighs 130 g I think is extraordinary progress, but certainly not where we want to get to longer term.
turns.zh: 我们大致认为 2030 年将是眼镜变得足够强大、足够便宜、足够可穿戴的十年。它们现在仍然要 2200 美元，所以价格点相当高，可穿戴性也还不够。今天大约 130 克，对比一下，Vision Pro 总重大概 2 磅。所以在一副 130 克的透明眼镜中拥有 Vision Pro 级别的能力，我认为是非凡的进步，但肯定不是我们长期想要达到的目标。

transcript.secZh: 可穿戴设备的挑战与未来

turns.en: Talking about social media, obviously you've been at this coal face for a long time and I've been covering a lot of the cases that have—I mean, there is just an avalanche of cases aimed at you at Meta, at TikTok, at YouTube. And you've agreed a series of settlements over the alleged addictive design brought by teenagers, by school districts, etc. And there's a growing sense, at least in the US, that social media is like the new tobacco, especially for kids. And that we're heading toward a moment where we're going to have some type of big tobacco type settlement, a big master fund to figure out how to deal with all the social consequences of this very powerful technology. I'm just wondering what is your view of where we are in that journey, especially when we look at a lot of these bans for under 16s that are starting to be rolled out around the world. Where do you think we are and do you think it's appropriate and where do you think we're going?
turns.zh: 谈到社交媒体，显然你在这个领域工作了很长时间，而我一直在报道很多案件——我的意思是，针对你们、Meta、TikTok、YouTube 的案件铺天盖地。你们已经就青少年、学区等提出的涉嫌成瘾性设计的指控达成了一系列和解。至少在美国，越来越多的人认为社交媒体就像新型烟草，尤其是对孩子们来说。我们正走向一个时刻，我们将达成某种类似大烟草和解的协议，建立一个大型总基金，以弄清楚如何应对这项非常强大技术的所有社会后果。我只是想知道你对我们在这一进程中处于什么位置的看法，特别是当我们看到世界各地开始推出针对 16 岁以下人群的禁令时。你认为我们处于什么位置，你认为这些禁令合适吗，你认为我们将走向何方？

turns.en: Well, I think it's appropriate to be concerned about the type of technology that we integrate into our lives and we should be very thoughtful about that. When it comes to Snapchat, one of the things we've really tried to help people understand is how different Snapchat is from social media. It's primarily used for messaging, primarily between a single digit number of close friends. And I think, when used responsibly, Snapchat can be really positive for people's well-being. And in fact, that's been proven out by the research. And so independent research shows when you can compare Snapchat to a TikTok or an Instagram or something like that, that Snapchat actually has a measured positive impact on people's well-being while those other services do not. And so one of the challenges that we've had—I think a lot of the social media skepticism and concern is oriented around Meta and their practices. We need to help people understand how different Snapchat is in terms of its functionality and also the extraordinary efforts we've undertaken over the last 15 years to help keep people safe on our service. So two people have to add each other as friends before they communicate. We invest really heavily in finding bad guys and removing them from our service and increasingly are able to do that with artificial intelligence. And so we've really worked hard to make Snapchat safe and certainly a lot here with the regulators in the UK. So, we've got four boys at home including one 15-year-old. And so as we think about building the service, it's incredibly important to me that he's safe when he's using Snapchat, his friends are. And it's certainly something we think about all the time.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为对我们融入生活的技术类型感到担忧是合适的，我们应该非常深思熟虑。说到 Snapchat，我们真正试图帮助人们理解的一件事是 Snapchat 与社交媒体有多么不同。它主要用于消息传递，主要是在个位数的亲密朋友之间。而且我认为，当负责任地使用时，Snapchat 可以对人们的福祉产生真正积极的影响。事实上，研究已经证明了这一点。独立研究表明，当你将 Snapchat 与 TikTok 或 Instagram 之类的服务进行比较时，Snapchat 实际上对人们的福祉有可衡量的积极影响，而其他服务则没有。所以我们面临的挑战之一——我认为很多对社交媒体的怀疑和担忧都围绕 Meta 及其做法。我们需要帮助人们理解 Snapchat 在功能上的不同，以及我们在过去 15 年为帮助确保用户安全所做的非凡努力。所以两个人必须互相添加为好友才能交流。我们大力投资于发现坏人并将他们从我们的服务中移除，并且越来越能够通过人工智能做到这一点。所以我们真的努力使 Snapchat 安全，在英国与监管机构也做了很多工作。所以，我们有四个男孩，包括一个 15 岁的孩子。所以当我们考虑构建服务时，对我来说，确保他在使用 Snapchat 时的安全非常重要，他的朋友们也是如此。这当然是我们一直考虑的事情。

transcript.secZh: 社交媒体与青少年安全

turns.en: As I said, there are thousands and thousands of legal cases still to come, right? That there's like there's just a big queue. Is the idea that basically you think you guys kind of stand apart from the folks like Meta? Because I think it's really interesting Meta, they struck this very public, very big settlement. I think it was $12 billion to settle a bunch of charges around how they design their apps and now they're advertising how they are leading the charge in terms of protecting teens. Could you talk a little bit about just that competitive dynamic because it does feel like especially teens on social media that is where a lot of the energy is both in terms of regulators and also parents.
turns.zh: 正如我所说，还有成千上万的法律案件即将到来，对吧？就像有一个大队列。是不是基本上你认为你们与 Meta 那些人不同？因为我觉得很有趣，Meta 达成了非常公开、非常大的和解。我想是 120 亿美元，以解决一系列关于他们如何设计应用的指控，现在他们正在宣传他们如何在保护青少年方面带头。你能谈谈这种竞争动态吗，因为确实感觉尤其是社交媒体上的青少年，这是监管机构和父母很多精力的所在。

turns.en: We really believe that collaboration is important when it comes to teen safety. In fact, we've overcome our differences and partnered with Meta on a lot of initiatives to help keep young people safe, including signal sharing.
turns.zh: 我们真的相信在青少年安全方面合作很重要。事实上，我们克服了分歧，与 Meta 合作了许多倡议，以帮助保护年轻人的安全，包括信号共享。

turns.en: So one of the challenging issues the platforms have is when you identify bad behavior and remove someone from your service, they can go hop to another service, right? And so unless companies actually work together to trace those folks across services and keep them off these platforms, it's hard to keep young people safe. So you guys do that kind of information sharing amongst each other?
turns.zh: 所以平台面临的一个挑战性问题是，当你发现不良行为并将某人从你的服务中移除时，他们可以跳到另一个服务，对吧？所以除非公司真正合作，跨服务追踪这些人并让他们远离这些平台，否则很难保护年轻人的安全。所以你们之间会进行那种信息共享吗？

turns.en: Exactly. Yeah. So that's one example, but I think ultimately collaboration's very important. I think Meta certainly feels that way and other folks in the industry do as well. I think this is an area where we're continuing to evolve, continuing to learn. And I think one of the most important breakthroughs as I mentioned really is the advancements in artificial intelligence, right? If you think about the regulatory framework of the past 10 years, I think it's really been focused on individual features of different services. And as I look at what we're doing now and the way we can make an impact in the future of safety, a lot of what's happening today is because on a technology service, everyone's behavior is entirely observable, right? You can find patterns of bad behavior very quickly and actually intervene before bad things happen. And so I think while the prior model was based on assessing the risk of various features, what is increasingly clear to me in the work that we're doing is that investments in really understanding user behavior across the service and intervening before bad things happen is the future of safety.
turns.zh: 没错。是的。所以那是一个例子，但我认为最终合作非常重要。Meta 当然有这种感觉，行业中的其他人也是如此。我认为这是一个我们正在不断进化、不断学习的领域。而且我认为最重要的突破之一，正如我提到的，真的是人工智能的进步，对吧？如果你想想过去 10 年的监管框架，我认为它真的专注于不同服务的个别功能。而当我审视我们现在所做的以及我们能在安全未来产生影响的方式时，今天发生的很多事情是因为在技术服务上，每个人的行为都是完全可观察的，对吧？你可以很快发现不良行为的模式，并在坏事发生之前进行干预。所以我认为，虽然之前的模型是基于评估各种功能的风险，但在我们所做的工作中越来越清楚的是，投资于真正理解用户在整个服务中的行为并在坏事发生之前进行干预，是安全的未来。

turns.en: I'm really interested to ask you about the political climate in the US. It's a great chance, you know, having you here in London. We'll swing out in a sec. Um you know we obviously saw the blue wave in the midterms last week, but also there was a backlash against tech and data centers. And I just wondered how that feels in Silicon Valley and has that changed your world at all?
turns.zh: 我真的很想问问你关于美国的政治气候。这是一个很好的机会，你知道，让你来到伦敦。我们稍后会转向那个话题。嗯，你知道我们显然看到了上周中期选举的蓝色浪潮，但同时也出现了对科技和数据中心的反弹。我只是想知道这在硅谷感觉如何，那是否改变了你的世界？

turns.en: Um well you know the backlash against AI is not new. This is something that we've been talking about for many years. It's something we saw very early on on our service, you know, because so many people are using our service and talking to one another and sharing videos. We can see very early on trends in how people feel about different things. And one of the things that was staggering to us was the amount of negativity around artificial intelligence. And in fact, it's one of the things that prompted us very early on to remove AI generated content from our service and to focus on real videos made by real people, which it turns out is really what our community wanted. And so this is not new. It's not a surprise. I think there is a lot of anxiety around AI right now, you know, not in small part due to the fact that the most prominent leaders in AI have been saying it's going to kill us all. So
turns.zh: 嗯，你知道对 AI 的反弹并不是新鲜事。这是我们多年来一直在谈论的事情。我们在我们的服务上很早就看到了这一点，因为这么多人在使用我们的服务，互相交谈，分享视频。我们可以很早就看到人们对不同事物的感受趋势。而让我们震惊的一件事是围绕人工智能的负面情绪之多。事实上，这是促使我们很早就从我们的服务中移除 AI 生成内容并专注于真实的人制作的真实视频的原因之一，事实证明这正是我们的社区想要的。所以这不是新的。这并不奇怪。我认为现在围绕 AI 有很多焦虑，你知道，很大程度上是因为 AI 领域最杰出的领导者们一直在说它会杀死我们所有人。所以

turns.en: Is it going to kill us all?
turns.zh: 它会杀死我们所有人吗？

turns.en: I certainly don't think so. No.
turns.zh: 我当然不这么认为。不。

turns.en: Um just speaking about kind of your evolution as a company, is the idea that effective what you're trying to effectuate is a we're trying to abstract away the screen and you know because with the arrival of AI you can now talk to your machine. You don't even have to type as much. And then if you have really capable glasses, maybe you don't this phone. Like, do you want to kill the smartphone?
turns.zh: 嗯，就你们作为一家公司的演变而言，是不是说你们试图实现的是抽象掉屏幕，你知道，因为随着 AI 的到来，你现在可以跟你的机器说话。你甚至不必打那么多字。然后如果你有非常能干的眼镜，也许你就不需要这个手机了。就像，你想杀死智能手机吗？

turns.en: Um, I don't think we're going to replace the phone anytime soon. I do think though, to your point, the way that we're using computers is really changing. And it's unlikely that 10 or 20 years from now we're going to be spending a lot of time behind our desks controlling a computer because as it turns out, AI is very likely to be much better at controlling computers than we are. And so I think that does mean that the form factor really can change. And there are some really big benefits of glasses like you mentioned. You know, they're next to all of our major sensory organs, right? Our ability to see and to hear um, those are things that you know, if you have a computer situated closer to your eyes, to your ears, I think can really make a positive impact on the computing experience, but only if it helps bring computing into the world. And ultimately, as you said, I think really to get out of the way and provide that sort of flexibility. And you know, I think part of this has to do also with the nature of how work is going to change, right? Because if we're spending less time sitting in front of a computer, I think there's a real opportunity and certainly I know the UK is focused on this, but in the US as well, on job skills, on reindustrialization. And I think it's going to be really important for people to get that sort of computer guidance, but on real world tasks. Um, and that's I think a huge opportunity for augmented reality and glasses and certainly something a lot of our partners are thinking about.
turns.zh: 嗯，我不认为我们会在短期内取代手机。但我确实认为，正如你所说，我们使用电脑的方式真的在改变。而且 10 年或 20 年后，我们不太可能花很多时间坐在桌子后面控制电脑，因为事实证明，AI 很可能比我们更擅长控制电脑。所以我认为这确实意味着形态真的可以改变。而且像你提到的，眼镜有一些非常大的好处。你知道，它们紧挨着我们所有的主要感觉器官，对吧？我们看和听的能力，嗯，那些是，你知道，如果你有一个电脑放在更靠近你的眼睛、你的耳朵的地方，我认为真的可以对计算体验产生积极影响，但前提是它有助于将计算带入世界。最终，正如你所说，我认为真的是要退到一边，提供那种灵活性。而且你知道，我认为这部分也与工作将如何改变的性质有关，对吧？因为如果我们花更少的时间坐在电脑前，我认为有一个真正的机会，当然我知道英国正在关注这一点，但在美国也是如此，关于工作技能，关于再工业化。而且我认为让人们获得那种电脑指导，但是在现实世界的任务上，将非常重要。嗯，我认为这是增强现实和眼镜的巨大机会，当然也是我们许多合作伙伴正在思考的事情。

transcript.secZh: 计算与智能手机的演进

turns.en: And how is AI changing Snap and changing what you do?
turns.zh: 那么 AI 如何改变 Snap 并改变你们所做的工作？

turns.en: AI's a really big deal for us because one, we have a network effects business, which makes it a lot harder for AI to just copy the software service that we created. So if you think about, you know, for a very long time, Meta's a really tough competitor. They copy virtually everything we do. And so we've thought a lot
turns.zh: AI 对我们来说非常重要，因为第一，我们有一个网络效应业务，这使得 AI 很难直接复制我们创建的软件服务。所以如果你想想，你知道，很长一段时间以来，Meta 是一个非常难对付的竞争对手。他们几乎复制我们所做的一切。所以我们想了很多

turns.en: They used to call you like Evan Spiegel, the R and D department for Mark Zuckerberg, right? Cuz he would just copy everything that you came up with.
turns.zh: 他们过去叫你埃文·斯皮格尔，马克·扎克伯格的研发部门，对吧？因为他会直接复制你提出的所有东西。

turns.en: Yeah, they still do. Yeah. Um, so we thought very early on about how to build a resilient service and a differentiated service, which I think is really serving us well in this moment in time when people are realizing that software businesses are very vulnerable. And you know, the user interface itself is changing. So I think the durability of friends talking to friends and that network is something that's really important to us. And that's allowed us to spend a lot more of our time instead of playing defensively like I think a lot of software businesses are right now, playing more offensively and thinking about how AI can transform how we work. And so as I look at, you know, our engineering teams, the number of merge pull requests, you know, basically code changes that have been submitted have doubled year on year even as the size of our team has declined by about 30%. So I think, you know, that sort of productivity growth is really meaningful for us as we're trying to compete with these huge companies with tons of resources.
turns.zh: 是的，他们仍然如此。是的。嗯，所以我们很早就思考了如何建立一个有弹性的服务和差异化的服务，我认为这在当下这个人们意识到软件业务非常脆弱的时刻真的对我们很有帮助。而且你知道，用户界面本身也在改变。所以我认为朋友之间交谈和那个网络的持久性对我们来说非常重要。这让我们能够花更多的时间，而不是像我认为现在许多软件企业那样采取防守，而是更多地采取进攻，思考 AI 如何改变我们的工作方式。所以当我审视我们的工程团队时，合并拉取请求的数量，基本上提交的代码更改同比翻了一番，即使我们团队的规模减少了约 30%。所以我认为，这种生产力增长对我们来说真的很有意义，因为我们正试图与这些拥有大量资源的巨大公司竞争。

turns.en: Should we take some questions from the audience? That's all right. Probably inevitably, and I'm sure you get asked this a lot. What do you make of the privacy concerns that have emerged out of the release of Ray-Ban Meta's fears that people will be filmed without their consent or knowledge?
turns.zh: 我们是不是该回答一些观众提问？好的。这个问题可能不可避免，我肯定你经常被问到。你如何看待 Ray-Ban Meta 发布后引发的隐私担忧——人们担心自己会在不知情或未经同意的情况下被拍摄？

turns.en: Yeah, I think it's really weird that they made spy glasses. We're not into that. And I think they made this whole show of disguising them like normal glasses, which made it all way worse. And I think what's so interesting, we made our first camera glasses a decade ago. But when we did that, we put a big yellow ring around it and had a very distinctive style, and people thought it was really fun. They'd be like, oh, are those camera glasses? Those are cool. Can I try? Because we weren't trying to hide the fact that they could be used to take photos. And I think that similar strategy applies here with specs. They're unmistakable, hard to miss from a mile away. And so I think to me that the sort of trust that is established in those key design choices really matters. And I think unfortunately, those choices have sort of set back the progress here in this area. I think, you know, one of the things people really like about Snap is they trust us with their private information. We were the leaders, for example, in data deletion way back in the day. And you know, that was back when actually it was more expensive to delete things because you had to overwrite the hard drive. And so no one deleted anything. They just said we'll store it forever. And so that we really pushed there on the ads front as well. I think we've really tried to be disciplined in the way that we use people's data to improve their experience on Snapchat. So all this to say we've thought a lot about how that applies to specs as well. And so things like on-device processing, very clear notifications around anything that involves recording, and then lots of restrictions around developer access I think are really important.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得他们做间谍眼镜真的很奇怪。我们不搞那一套。而且我觉得他们故意把它们伪装成普通眼镜，这反而让情况更糟。有趣的是，我们十年前就做了第一款相机眼镜。但当时我们在镜框上放了一个大黄色圆环，设计风格非常独特，人们觉得很有趣。他们会说，哦，那是相机眼镜吗？很酷，我能试试吗？因为我们并没有试图隐藏它们可以拍照的事实。我认为类似的策略也适用于 Specs。它们一眼就能认出来，从一英里外都很难错过。所以对我来说，这些关键设计选择中建立的信任非常重要。不幸的是，那些选择让这个领域的进展倒退了。我觉得人们喜欢 Snap 的一点是，他们信任我们处理他们的私人信息。例如，我们很早就是数据删除方面的领导者。那时候删除数据实际上更贵，因为必须覆盖硬盘。所以没人删除任何东西，他们只说我们会永远存储。因此我们在广告方面也真正推动了这一点。我认为我们一直努力在利用人们数据改善 Snapchat 体验方面保持自律。所以总而言之，我们对于如何将其应用于 Specs 也思考了很多。因此，设备端处理、任何涉及录制的非常清晰的提示，以及对开发者访问的许多限制，我认为都非常重要。

transcript.sec: Tech for Kids and AI Education

turns.en: Thank you. You mentioned your kids earlier. I know this is probably a question that's relevant to a lot of people in the room. How should we think now about tech for our kids? And what are you teaching or telling your kids, particularly about AI?
turns.zh: 谢谢。你之前提到了你的孩子。我知道这可能是现场很多人都关心的问题。我们现在应该如何思考给孩子用的科技产品？你特别在教或告诉你的孩子关于 AI 的什么？

turns.en: Yeah, you know, it's so interesting because it really feels like culture has sort of ebbed and flowed on this. When I was growing up, adults were telling us all the time that we had to embrace technology, learn how to use computers, how transformative it would be, how transformative the internet could be. And that made a hugely positive impact on my life. And so I've taken a lot of those lessons in terms of how we approach it with our kids. And I think for them to see tools like AI, they can take an idea that's in their mind and make it a real thing in a couple of minutes. I mean, they can brainstorm an idea for a game they want to play and have the game. And I think that sort of feedback loop of being able to imagine and create so quickly is something that's really inspiring for young people and also just lowers the bar when they think about their future and what they can create in the world. So it's been really important for us to teach our kids about AI, also to teach them about the risks involved with technology, of course. But I would say I'm hugely optimistic about the role of technology in transforming the world.
turns.zh: 是的，你知道，这很有趣，因为文化在这方面的态度真的起起伏伏。我成长的时候，大人们总是告诉我们必须拥抱技术，学习如何使用电脑，它会有多大的变革性，互联网会有多大的变革性。这对我的生活产生了巨大的积极影响。所以我从中吸取了很多教训，用来对待我们的孩子。我认为让他们看到像 AI 这样的工具，他们可以在几分钟内把脑海中的想法变成现实。我的意思是，他们可以头脑风暴一个想玩的游戏创意，然后就有了这个游戏。我认为这种能够如此快速地想象和创造的反馈循环，对年轻人来说非常鼓舞人心，也降低了他们思考未来和他们在世界上能创造什么的门槛。所以教我们的孩子关于 AI 的知识非常重要，当然也要教他们技术的风险。但我想说，我对技术改变世界的作用非常乐观。

turns.en: I have a question as a fellow Californian. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, failed. I think they've officially called it today. So two questions. One, you obviously stayed in California when a lot of people left, especially in the tech industry. Why did you stay? And what do you think it says about this moment that they're talking about trying again? And there's a lot of anger against what you call the billionaire class, the elite class, whatever, the bro-ligarchy. I'm not saying you're a bro-ligarch. But you know, so why did you stay and what do you think this, the fact that it got on the ballot says about this moment?
turns.zh: 作为一个加州同胞，我有个问题。40 号提案，也就是亿万富翁税，失败了。我想他们今天正式宣布了。所以两个问题。第一，显然当很多人离开时你留在了加州，尤其是在科技行业。你为什么留下？以及他们正在讨论再次尝试，你认为这说明了这个时代的什么？有很多愤怒针对你所说的亿万富翁阶层、精英阶层，随便什么，兄弟寡头。我不是说你是兄弟寡头。但你知道，所以你为什么留下，以及它出现在选票上这件事，你认为说明了这个时代的什么？

turns.en: Oh, there's a lot to unpack here. What do I think? So first of all, I love California and that's why I want to stay. I grew up in Los Angeles. My friends from high school are there, my parents are there. So I really love the community that we're in and I wouldn't trade that for Miami, I guess, at this point. But I think it raised some good questions. I think however, that California voters aren't dumb and they were very concerned about the long-term impacts of something like Prop 40 because it was very clear from the data that it actually reduced tax revenues over time. So if you're going to reduce tax revenues and very wealthy people are going to leave California, then who is going to be stuck paying all the taxes? And so I think your average voter was really actually able to understand that. At the same time, I think there's a lot of anger and frustration about perceived extraordinary inequality at a time when young people don't feel like they can get ahead. I think this is one of the first generations that feels like they won't be better off than their parents. I think we're at a time, certainly in the United States, I'm not sure the latest metrics here in the UK, but our federal government invests $7 in old people for every $1 in young people. And that is felt, I think, very deeply in our country. And so there's a lot of frustration around young people, around the demographic shifts that I think are really straining their ability to succeed.
turns.zh: 哦，这里有很多要分析的。我怎么想？首先，我爱加州，这就是我想留下的原因。我在洛杉矶长大。我高中的朋友在那里，我的父母在那里。所以我真的很喜欢我们所在的社区，我想在这一点上我不会拿它换迈阿密。但我认为它提出了一些好问题。不过我认为加州选民不傻，他们非常担心像 40 号提案这样的东西的长期影响，因为数据非常清楚，它实际上随着时间的推移减少了税收。所以如果你要减少税收，非常富有的人要离开加州，那么谁会留下来支付所有税收？所以我认为普通选民实际上能够理解这一点。与此同时，我认为人们对于感知到的极端不平等有很多愤怒和沮丧，尤其是在年轻人觉得自己无法前进的时候。我认为这是第一批觉得自己不会比父母过得更好的世代之一。我认为我们正处于这样一个时代，当然在美国，我不确定英国的最新指标，但我们的联邦政府在老年人身上每花 7 美元，在年轻人身上只花 1 美元。我认为这在我们国家感受非常深刻。所以年轻人有很多沮丧，围绕人口结构变化，我认为这真的在削弱他们成功的能力。

transcript.sec: Use Cases and Revenue for Specs

turns.en: Well, let's finish with a couple of questions about the future of Snap from the audience. Someone's asking, what are the use cases for specs and what are the revenue streams going to be?
turns.zh: 好的，让我们以观众关于 Snap 未来的几个问题来结束。有人问，Specs 的用例有哪些，收入来源会是什么？

turns.en: Oh my gosh, there's so many use cases. I think there's everything from enterprise use cases like remote assistance where you're trying to solve a technical problem, you're keeping your hands free, someone who's back home can see what you're working on and guide you. You know, overlay arrows and things like that help you fix what you're working on. Certainly a lot of folks are building out agentic workflows. So again, if you're a maintenance technician, you can come in, look at something you're trying to fix, understand exactly what the product is, pull up the maintenance history.
turns.zh: 哦天哪，用例太多了。我认为从企业用例到远程协助，比如你试图解决一个技术问题，双手保持自由，家里的人可以看到你正在做什么并指导你。你知道，叠加箭头之类的东西帮助你修复你正在处理的东西。当然，很多人在构建智能体式工作流。再说一次，如果你是一名维护技术员，你可以进来，看看你要修的东西，准确了解产品是什么，调出维护历史。

turns.en: Again, all hands-free and stay focused on the task. I think from a more broad-based consumer perspective, there are a couple things that are really resonating with folks. One is having a giant, I mean, it's the equivalent of a 115-inch cinema display, high-resolution cinema display that you can bring with you anywhere. So that's everything from watching a movie on an airplane, again, not with VR shut off from the world, but see-through, or bringing a large portable display if you want to get work done and you want to get work done on a private display. I think that specs can be really meaningful for that. And then there's all sorts of what we call location-based experiences. So it can change the way that you explore a museum, for example, or a theme park and really bring those experiences to life in a way that's shared and immersive. So, there's that and then there's a zillion new things that developers are building. I mean, almost every day a developer is shipping something new for specs. So, it's pretty fun to follow that too.
turns.zh: 再次强调，这一切都是免手操作的，并且可以让你专注于任务。我认为从更广泛的消费者角度来看，有几件事确实引起了人们的共鸣。一是拥有一块巨大的、相当于 115 英寸影院显示屏的高分辨率影院级显示屏，而且你可以随身携带到任何地方。所以这涵盖了从在飞机上看电影——再次强调，不是用 VR 把自己与世界隔绝，而是透视式的——到如果你想完成工作，并且希望在私人显示屏上工作，就可以带上一块大型便携显示屏。我认为 specs 在这方面可以非常有意义。然后还有各种我们称之为基于位置的体验。所以它可以改变你探索博物馆或主题公园的方式，真正让这些体验以共享和沉浸的方式栩栩如生。所以，有这些，还有开发者正在构建的数不清的新东西。我的意思是，几乎每天都有开发者为 specs 发布新东西。所以，关注这些也很有趣。

turns.en: I had a great question about advertising. As more AI agents browse the web, how do you expect that to affect what advertisers are willing to pay for ads? So, what are you seeing?
turns.zh: 我有一个关于广告的好问题。随着越来越多的 AI 智能体浏览网页，您预计这会如何影响广告商愿意为广告支付的费用？那么，您看到了什么？

turns.en: Yeah, that's such a good question. So, we're Snap's more of a walled garden and we do a lot of work to authenticate our audience and make sure that real people instead of agents are using our service. But I think if I look at what advertisers are optimizing for today, typically they're lower funnel goals and that's really where we focus. So, 77% of our business is direct response, meaning buying a product online or making a purchase. And advertisers are very disciplined in measuring that, doing the technical work to understand the impact that our systems can drive for them. So, I think that's just going to continue to be the case. So, regardless of whatever agent traffic is on the web, I think that the winning advertising platforms are going to be the ones that really demonstrate business results in terms of driving conversions.
turns.zh: 是的，这个问题非常好。Snap 更像是一个围墙花园，我们做了大量工作来验证我们的受众，确保是真实的人而不是智能体在使用我们的服务。但我认为，如果看看广告商今天在优化什么，通常是下层漏斗目标，而这正是我们关注的。所以，我们 77% 的业务是直接响应，也就是在线购买产品或完成购买。广告商在衡量这一点上非常自律，他们会做技术工作来了解我们的系统能为他们带来什么影响。所以，我认为这种情况只会继续下去。因此，无论网上有多少智能体流量，我认为获胜的广告平台将是那些真正能展示推动转化方面业务成果的平台。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.zh: 太棒了。好吧，我想时间到了，可惜时间过得真快。但请大家和我一起感谢 Evan 来到这里。真是太棒了。你觉得我们的朋友 Evan 怎么样？

Ofcom stats show that a third of 8 to 12 year olds are on Snapchat.

turns.en: A third of 8 to 12 year olds.
turns.zh: 三分之一 8 到 12 岁的孩子。

turns.en: So, that remains a problem for the company and for the regulator. Now, when you speak to the company about it, they say, look, we are trying our best. Parents need to take responsibility for changing the settings on devices. You know, there's only so much social media companies can do.
turns.zh: 所以，这对公司和监管机构来说仍然是个问题。现在，当你和公司谈论这件事时，他们会说，看，我们正在尽力。父母需要负责更改设备上的设置。你知道，社交媒体公司能做的有限。

turns.en: That stat before we got on stage with them. I that's an extraordinary stat.
turns.zh: 那个统计数据是在我们上台之前。我觉得那是个非同寻常的统计数据。

turns.en: So I should say that's in the UK, but it's a big number. As you know, it's a very sensitive time. The Online Safety Bill has been introduced here. So they're really cracking down on social media companies. I do feel that you and I are quite lucky as parents of younger children that the mood music it seems to me is changing not only here in the UK, but also in the US following the recent meta settlement. And as we discussed the TikTok and Snap as well, that it's becoming less normal just to chuck your kid a smartphone at 11 and allow them onto social media. And it is actually very helpful to have the voice of the regulator. And I know when I'm talking to my kids and so it's not allowed.
turns.zh: 所以我应该说明那是在英国，但这是个很大的数字。如你所知，这是一个非常敏感的时期。这里已经出台了《在线安全法案》。所以他们真的在严厉打击社交媒体公司。我确实觉得，作为年幼孩子的父母，你和我很幸运，在我看来，不仅在英国，而且在最近 Meta 和解之后在美国，氛围正在改变。正如我们讨论过的 TikTok 和 Snap，在 11 岁时随便给孩子一部智能手机并允许他们使用社交媒体变得越来越不寻常。实际上，有监管机构的声音非常有帮助。我知道当我和孩子们交谈时，所以这是不允许的。

turns.zh: 还没有。他们没有智能手机。

turns.zh: 昨天很多人对我的 Instinct 智能体非常感兴趣。我想，对你来说可能很难理解，因为你那里每个人都在用它们。但它们

tldr.zh: Snap CEO 埃文·斯皮格尔押注计算将转向共享、免手的 AR 眼镜，让科技更人性化。
